summary:
Article 120 of Uzbekistan's 1994 Criminal Code criminalises consensual sexual conduct between men and provides for up to three years' imprisonment. Human Dignity Trust's country profile, Human Rights Watch's World Report 2024 (covering events of 2023) and the UK Home Office's country-policy and information note of July 2024 all record the offence as in force. The Home Office documents cases prosecuted under Article 120 between 2009 and 2023, so the provision is applied rather than dormant; 2023 is the most recent documented case in this record.

Human Rights Watch reports that police target gay and bisexual men and trans women with arbitrary detention, prosecution and imprisonment. The same report records that forced examinations carried out in these cases amount to torture under WHO definition, and that impunity for police ill-treatment persists. The Home Office describes police intimidation, violence and exploitation of gay men and trans people as routine.

The US State Department's 2023 human-rights report records that LGBTQI+ people are arrested and then released, or threatened with arrest unless they pay bribes, and that police coerce LGBTQI+ people into informing on others under threat of prison. Its 2021 report, covering an earlier period, records torture and ill-treatment and arbitrary detention in custody alongside social stigma and violence against LGBT people under the criminalised framework. Human Rights Watch reported in March 2021 that gay and bisexual men face discrimination, violence, blackmail and extortion from both state and non-state actors with almost no legal protection.

Official hostility is on the record. In April 2023 Uzbekistan's constitution was adopted with sexual orientation deliberately omitted from the list of protected characteristics, which did include gender, race, religion and nationality. In November 2024 the leader of the Milliy Tiklanish party announced he was drafting a law banning discussion of LGBTQ people, stating that it was inspired by statements made by Ivanka Trump about "LGBT propaganda" in schools.

LGBTI organisations cannot register in Uzbekistan and operate unofficially, according to the July 2024 Home Office note, which also reports that a rural taboo drives discrimination. The US State Department's 2023 report records continuing societal harassment.
tangentialFactors:
The US State Department's 2023 report notes that websites and bloggers self-censor on LGBTQI+ issues, which narrows the public availability of information a visitor can rely on locally.

Human Rights Watch's March 2021 statement urged decriminalisation while Uzbekistan held a seat on the UN Human Rights Council, an advocacy milestone rather than a change in the law; Article 120 remained in force in the July 2024 Home Office note.

ECOM's 2024 national report covers Uzbekistan's legislation, anti-discrimination provisions, criminalisation of HIV transmission, legal gender recognition, access to human rights, and the rights to health and work. The inventory supplies the report's scope but none of its findings, so no substantive claim from it can be carried here.
localsOnly:
Residents face the coercive use of Article 120 as leverage: the US State Department's 2023 report documents police compelling LGBTQI+ people to inform on others under threat of prison, and arresting or threatening arrest in order to extract bribes.

LGBTI organisations cannot register and operate unofficially, leaving residents without a lawful associational channel for complaint or advocacy, per the July 2024 Home Office note.

The April 2023 constitutional text omits sexual orientation from its protected characteristics while listing gender, race, religion and nationality, so residents have no constitutional anchor for a discrimination claim on that ground.

Discrimination is reported as driven in particular by rural taboos (Home Office, July 2024), and societal harassment continued as of the US State Department's 2023 report.
outOfScopeNotes:
Legal gender recognition is unresolved in this inventory. ECOM's 2024 national report is listed as examining legal gender recognition, but no finding from it is supplied, and no other source here states whether change of legal sex is available or refused. The same applies to entry and visa rules, document markers, airport screening treatment of gender-nonconforming travellers, bathroom and facilities rules, and access to gender-affirming care: no source in this inventory addresses them.

The November 2024 announcement of a bill banning discussion of LGBTQ people is sourced only to Wikipedia's country coverage. Whether the bill was introduced, passed or abandoned is not established here, and the claim should be treated as unverified pending a primary source.

The most recent documented prosecution under Article 120 in this record is from 2023; no later case is documented. Absence of a later case is not evidence that prosecutions have stopped.

No figures for trans-specific violence appear in this inventory, so no comparison with Uzbekistan's general homicide rate can be made.
